body_html:
Este, ese, aquel are the Spanish words for “this” and “that”, and the difference is distance. English has two levels (this, that); Spanish has three. Este is near the speaker, ese is near the listener or a bit further away, and aquel is far from both. They also change for gender and number, and there are neuter forms (esto, eso, aquello) for ideas and unknown things. It sounds like a lot, but the system is very regular.

Quick answer
  • Este = this (near me): este libro.
  • Ese = that (near you, or not far): ese libro.
  • Aquel = that over there (far from both): aquel edificio.
  • Esto, eso, aquello = this, that (things you can’t name, ideas).
{{toc}}

Este, ese, aquel: all the forms

Near meNear you / middleFar from both
Masc. sing.esteeseaquel
Fem. sing.estaesaaquella
Masc. pl.estosesosaquellos
Fem. pl.estasesasaquellas
Neuterestoesoaquello

A useful link with adverbs: este goes with aquí, ese with ahí, and aquel with allí or allá. See {{link:aqui-vs-aca|aquí vs acá}}.

Este: near the speaker

  • Este café está buenísimo. This coffee is delicious (the one in my hand).
  • Esta semana trabajo mucho. I’m working a lot this week (time).
  • Estos zapatos me quedan grandes. These shoes are too big for me.

Ese: near the listener, or not far

  • ¿Me pasas esa botella? Can you pass me that bottle (near you)?
  • Ese chico de ahí es mi primo. That guy there is my cousin.
  • Esa idea que tuviste es genial. That idea you had is great (mentioned before).

In everyday speech, ese is by far the most common “that”, used for anything not right next to you.

{{image:2}}

Aquel: far away in space or time

  • ¿Ves aquella montaña? Do you see that mountain (over there)?
  • En aquella época no había celulares. Back then there were no cell phones.
  • Aquellos años fueron los mejores. Those years were the best.

Aquel often adds a nostalgic, distant feeling when talking about the past.

Esto, eso, aquello: the neuter forms

Use the neuter forms when you don’t know or don’t name the thing, or to refer to an idea or situation:

  • ¿Qué es esto? What is this?
  • Eso no es verdad. That isn’t true.
  • Aquello fue un desastre. That was a disaster.
  • ¡Eso es! That’s it! / Exactly!

Neuter forms never go before a noun and never take a written accent.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

What about accents (éste, ése)?

You may see éste, ése, aquél with accents in older texts, used when the demonstrative replaces a noun. Since 2010, the RAE recommends writing them without accents in all cases: Me gusta este, pero prefiero ese. The RAE’s guidance on the written accent explains that this accent is unnecessary, even in the rare cases where a sentence could be ambiguous.

Why this is tricky for learners

English “that” covers both ese and aquel, so learners either use ese for everything (which is mostly fine) or overuse aquel after learning it. The truth is that aquel is less common in conversation, especially in Latin America, where ese covers a lot of ground. The other trap is gender: English “this” never changes, but Spanish demonstratives agree with the noun, so esta mesa but este problema (remember, problema is masculine; see {{link:spanish-gender-mistakes|Spanish gender mistakes}}).

Real conversations

At a market

  • Customer: ¿Cuánto cuestan estas naranjas? (How much are these oranges?)
  • Seller: Esas, a cuarenta pesos el kilo. Y aquellas del fondo, a treinta. (Those are forty pesos a kilo. And those at the back, thirty.)
  • Customer: Pues deme un kilo de esas, por favor. (Then give me a kilo of those, please.)

Looking at old photos

  • A: ¿Y esto? ¿Dónde fue? (And this? Where was it?)
  • B: Eso fue en Cádiz. ¡Aquel verano fue increíble! (That was in Cádiz. That summer was amazing!)

Notice how the seller uses esas for the oranges near the customer, and how aquel verano adds a touch of nostalgia.

Try it yourself

  1. This house is old. (Esta casa es vieja.)
  2. Can you give me that pen (near you)? (¿Me das esa pluma?)
  3. Those mountains over there are the Andes. (Aquellas montañas son los Andes.)
  4. What’s that? (¿Qué es eso?)
  5. In those days we lived in Seville. (En aquellos tiempos vivíamos en Sevilla.)

More pairs in {{link:spanish-confusing-words|my complete list of Spanish confusing words}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Near me: este. Near you or not far: ese. Far from both, or long ago: aquel. Make them agree with the noun, use esto, eso, aquello for ideas and unknown things, and forget the old accents.

faq.q: What is the difference between este, ese and aquel?
faq.a: Este means this (near the speaker), ese means that (near the listener or not far) and aquel means that over there (far from both, or far in time).

faq.q: When do you use esto, eso and aquello?
faq.a: For things you can’t or don’t name, and for ideas or situations: ¿Qué es esto?, Eso no es verdad.

faq.q: Do éste and ése still have accents?
faq.a: No. Since 2010 the RAE recommends writing demonstratives without accents, even when they replace a noun.
